acceptedWorkstreams.title: Publish only the response-time commitment your own records already support
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A response-time promise is easy to write and expensive to break, so write it from evidence. Work: pull the last ninety days of support threads and incident notes, and record for each one the time from first report to first human reply, and from reply to fix. Report the distribution rather than the average, because the slow tail is what a buyer experiences. Then propose one commitment the team can meet four times out of five, with the measurement that proves it, and keep the raw table so it can be re-run each quarter. Deliver the table, the distribution, the proposed commitment and the sentence it replaces on the marketing site.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Publish the maintenance rule and the notice period as a commitment, not a habit
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Most status pages have no rule for planned work, so the first maintenance window is announced on the day and looks like an incident. Write the rule down before it is needed. Work: agree the notice period a customer gets before planned work, what counts as planned work versus an incident, where the notice appears (status page, in-app banner, email), and what happens if the work overruns. Then write the two template entries, one for a scheduled window and one for an overrun, and check them against a real past maintenance event the team can remember. Deliver the rule, both templates, and the note on which past event would have read differently under it.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Run one incident drill before publishing, so the first real one is not the rehearsal
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A status page is judged the first time it is used, and that is the worst time to discover the template is unclear or the update cadence is unagreed. Run one drill while nothing is broken. Work: pick a plausible incident, have the team write the opening update in the template, then write the two follow-ups, and time each step. Note where the wording stalls and who has to approve a public message. Deliver the drill transcript, the template change that came out of it, the named person who writes and publishes each update, and the honest answer to how long a first update would take on a real Saturday. No page is published without that answer.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Start the record from incidents the team can already confirm, and publish it as a dated log
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A status page that starts empty looks like a claim rather than a record, and one that starts with made-up history is worse. Start from what is already known. Work: 1) collect the incidents the team can confirm from the last few months: support threads, the team chat, and anything a customer reported twice, each with a date, an impact in plain words and how it was resolved; 2) design the page around four services a educator cares about (sign-in, channels, calls, file access) and state for each what a reader can expect; 3) write the incident template so future entries take two minutes and never contain customer names; 4) agree one response-time statement the team can actually meet, and write it in the terms the team agreed, not the terms marketing prefers; 5) cross-check every reliability line already on the marketing site against the record and list which now stand and which must be softened. Deliver: the page copy, the incident template, the dated log, and the claim-by-claim check.
